home_lede: Small, focused utilities for training and racing. Install it once and the tools keep working without a signal — only the YouTube picks need one.
metronome_info: Cadence is your steps per minute. A higher cadence means shorter steps and your foot landing closer under your body. Research shows this reduces overstriding, braking forces, and impact loading at the hip, knee, and ankle, which is linked to lower injury risk. Raising your natural cadence by 5–10% can cut peak knee impact by roughly 20% without costing extra energy. Many runners aim for 170–180 steps/min; studies found cadences at or above 170 associated with fewer overuse injuries. Increase gradually by about 5% at a time and let the metronome set the rhythm while you match each footstrike to a beat.
drink_session_hint: Pick the closest fit — the preset sets the carbohydrate and sodium targets the mix is built to hit.
drink_setup_hint: What you carry and how much you drink — the mix is sized to that.
drink_fluid_hint: Sweat rate is typically 0.5–2.0 L/h, higher in heat and at race pace — weigh yourself before and after a run to find yours.
drink_fluid_label: Your fluid intake in millilitres per hour
drink_potassium_hint: LoSalt ≈ 66 %, many reduced-sodium blends ≈ 30–50 %, your blend 33 %.
drink_potassium_label: Percentage of potassium chloride in your potassium-rich salt
drink_per_bottle_potassium: {tableSalt} g table salt + {potassiumSalt} g potassium salt + {sugar} g sugar
drink_schedule_bottle: Drink one {ml} ml bottle about every {minutes} minutes.
drink_schedule_stations: You carry {carry} ml but need about {need} ml. Pick up the remaining {short} ml at drink stations — about {sip} ml every {minutes} minutes — or carry an extra bottle.
drink_schedule_gels: Add about {gels} gel(s) (25 g each) to reach the {carbs} g/h carbohydrate target.
drink_schedule_sodium_short: Your bottles fall {mg} mg short of the sodium target for this session.
drink_info_targets: Targets follow the ACSM position stand on exercise and fluid replacement — 500–700 mg of sodium per litre and 600–1200 ml of fluid per hour for sessions over an hour, with 30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour as a 4–8% solution — and the 2016 joint position stand (ACSM / Dietitians of Canada / Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics), which raises carbohydrate to 30–90 g/h for longer sessions using multiple transportable carbohydrates. Sweat sodium varies from about 17 to 92 mmol/L between runners, so the Marathon preset mixes at ~1150 mg/L (50 mmol/L) — as concentrated as drinkable, since palatability falls beyond that. Table salt is ~393 mg sodium per gram; potassium chloride is ~524 mg potassium per gram, so a “reduced sodium” blend that is 33 % KCl provides ~263 mg sodium and ~173 mg potassium per gram.
drink_info_medical: If you have kidney problems, or take ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics or other medication that raises blood potassium, do not add a potassium-rich salt without medical advice. Weigh ingredients on a 0.1 g scale — household teaspoons vary.
drink_flag_carbs_capped: Carbs capped at 80 g/L (8% solution) so the drink stays drinkable. Your bottles cover {coverage} of the {plan} g plan — add about {gels} gel(s) (25 g each) or a third bottle.
drink_flag_sodium_capped: Sodium capped at 1150 mg/L (50 mmol/L — above that, drinks get unpalatable). Your bottles cover {coverage} of the {plan} mg plan — take the rest at drink stations or from a stronger mix.
drink_flag_fluid_short: Your {hours} h plan needs ~{need} ml of fluid but you carry {carry} ml. Take about {sip} ml every 15 min from drink stations, or carry an extra bottle.
drink_flag_hypertonic: This mix is hypertonic at {osmolality} mOsm/L — it leaves the stomach slowly. Chase each bottle with plain water.
drink_flag_dilute: Very dilute ({carbs} g carbs/L). Fine as a hydration drink, but a long session will need gels or food for carbohydrate.
drink_flag_low_sodium: Only {sodium} mg sodium/L. That is weaker than the 500–700 mg/L usually recommended for sessions over an hour.
drink_flag_fructose: Sucrose at {carbs} g/h delivers ~{fructose} g/h fructose, at the ~30 g/h fructose absorption ceiling. Normal for most runners, but the upper limit if you get gut trouble.
drink_flag_glucose: {carbs} g/h sucrose means ~{glucose} g/h glucose — above the ~60 g/h absorption ceiling. Gut training required.
drink_flag_overdrinking: Drinking over 1 L/h can dilute your blood sodium. Do not exceed your measured sweat rate.
drink_flag_underdrinking: Under 300 ml/h is unlikely to keep up with sweat losses — check your sweat rate by weighing yourself before and after a run.
drink_flag_potassium_overshoot: Your potassium-rich salt is {percent} KCl — hitting the sodium target with it already overshoots the potassium target, so no plain table salt is added.
drink_flag_potassium_low: Your potassium salt is only {percent} KCl, so it adds almost no potassium. Check the label.
race_recent_hint: What you have actually run — the fitness every number below comes from.
race_date_hint: The models assume you are as fit today as you were then.
race_time_hint: mm:ss or h:mm:ss — paste 1:32:00 as it comes.
race_goal_hint: The race you are planning — its pace, then its splits below.
race_goal_pace_hint: From your recent race — edit it to plan a different effort.
race_goal_pace_hint_custom: Your own pace. Use the predicted one to go back to the models.
race_vdot_sub: the fitness score your result implies
race_splits_at_prediction: at the Daniels prediction, the model the training paces come from
race_zone_easy_note: Conversational — the bulk of your week.
race_zone_marathon_note: Goal marathon pace; comfortably hard for hours.
race_zone_threshold_note: Comfortably hard, roughly a one-hour effort.
race_zone_interval_note: 3–5 minute reps at VO₂max; hard but repeatable.
race_zone_rep_note: Short fast reps for speed and economy; full recovery.
race_flag_future: That race date is in the future — a prediction needs a result you have already run.
race_flag_stale: That result is {weeks} weeks old. Treat the prediction as an upper bound: fitness decays when training drops, and the models assume you are as fit today as you were then.
race_flag_extrapolation: {goal} is more than {ratio}× away from {race}. Predictions degrade that far out — Riegel flatters a long race predicted from a short one, because it ignores the fuelling and durability that decide it.
race_flag_implausible: A VDOT of {vdot} is outside the plausible {min}–{max} band — check the distance and the time you entered.
race_flag_short: Under {distance} the Riegel exponent is a poor fit — it was derived from longer races, where fatigue rather than raw speed sets the time.
race_flag_ultra: Beyond {distance} aerobic fitness stops being the limiter: fuelling, terrain and time on feet decide the result, and neither model knows about them.
race_flag_spread: The two models disagree by {spread} at that distance. Read the prediction as a range between them rather than a target time.
race_flag_goal_faster_than_race: The goal pace ({goalPace}) is faster than your {race} pace ({racePace}) over a longer race — that is a time to re-check, not a target.
race_flag_goal_slower: Your goal pace is {percent} slower than the models predict for {goal} ({predictedPace}). The training paces above still come from your race fitness, not from this pace.
race_flag_goal_faster: Your goal pace is {percent} faster than the models predict for {goal} ({predictedPace}). The training paces above still come from your race fitness, not from this pace.
race_info_riegel: Two independent models, both fed the same result. Riegel (American Scientist, 1981) scales a performance by distance with a fatigue exponent: T₂ = T₁ × (D₂/D₁)1.06. That exponent is a population average — Riegel's own fits to running records span 1.05–1.08, and later work argues no single power law covers every distance — so it is fixed here rather than exposed as a dial.
race_info_daniels: Daniels & Gilbert's "Oxygen Power" regressions take the other route: they turn the result into a fitness score, VDOT, by dividing the oxygen cost of the race pace by the fraction of VO₂max sustainable for that long, then solve for the time at another distance. VDOT is also the number behind the training paces below. Across 5 km to the marathon the two models agree within about 1% for a typical result; the spread column is where they disagree, and a spread of more than a few percent is the model saying it is extrapolating.
race_info_paces: Training paces are Daniels' intensity bands — easy 59–74% of VDOT, marathon 75–84%, threshold 83–88%, interval 97–100%, repetition 105–110% — with the pace at each edge computed by inverting the VO₂ regression. The printed pace tables in the book sit at the hard end of those bands for marathon/threshold/interval/repetition, and print a narrower easy range (about 65–74%); the band shown here is the stated intensity range, so its easy end is genuinely easy.
race_info_splits: The splits are arithmetic on the plan's pace, not physiology. Even splits divide the plan's time by the distance. A negative split ramps the pace linearly so the second half averages 1.5% faster than the first — a plan you can run, rather than a step change at halfway. Splits are one unit each, and the final row absorbs the leftover metres, which is why it can read 1.1 km.
race_info_goal_pace: The goal pace starts as the models' prediction for that distance and is yours to edit — a slower plan pace is how you build in a margin. Editing it moves the goal time and every split with it; the training paces above do not move, because they describe what your race result makes you fit for rather than what you intend to run.
race_info_limits: What neither model knows: the weather, the course, the altitude, your fuelling, and whether you have trained for that distance at all. Treat a prediction as a target to aim at, and read the flags above as the places where it is being stretched.
taper_race_hint: The date and distance you are tapering for — the plan counts back from race day.
taper_training_hint: A normal week and how you split it — the taper cuts this volume, not your run count.
taper_normal_week_hint: Your average weekly distance in the weeks before the taper.
taper_runs_hint: Unchanged by the taper — the runs get shorter, not fewer.
taper_flag_past: This race date is in the past — pick an upcoming race for a schedule you can run.
taper_flag_under_way: The taper is already under way: today is day {day} of {days}. Earlier days are shown for reference.
taper_flag_race_longer_than_week: Your race ({race}) is longer than your normal training week ({week}). A taper makes you fresh, not fit — the volume has to be there first.
taper_flag_low_volume: Under {distance} a week there is little volume to shed: keep the taper short and change nothing else.
taper_flag_long_taper: Three weeks is a long taper at {week} a week. Two weeks is the meta-analysis optimum; three suits a high-volume marathon block.
taper_flag_short_race: Short races are usually tapered for one to two weeks; three weeks can leave you feeling stale.
taper_flag_cut_too_deep: The day layout cuts {percent} of your normal volume, deeper than the 41–60% the literature favours, because {runs} runs a week cannot absorb the planned days. Add a run day to hold more.
taper_flag_cut_too_shallow: The schedule cuts {percent} of your normal volume, less than the 41–60% band. Drop a run or shorten the easy days if you want a deeper taper.
taper_info_literature: A taper is a progressive, nonlinear cut in training load: keep the intensity, cut the volume, and cut it by a lot. Mujika & Padilla (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2003;35:1182–1187) describe it as maintaining training intensity, reducing training volume by up to 60–90% and trimming frequency by no more than 20%, over anything from 4 to more than 28 days, for a typical performance gain of about 3% (range 0.5–6.0%). The meta-analysis by Bosquet et al. (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39:1358–1365) narrows the optimum: a two-week taper in which training volume falls exponentially by 41–60%, with intensity and frequency unchanged.
taper_info_model: This planner decays your weekly training volume geometrically so that the volume over the whole taper window lands 50% below the same number of normal weeks — the middle of that 41–60% band — and reports the reduction it actually schedules, because the day layout can round it either way. Race day is not part of the training volume: race week is a short training week plus the race, which is why its total load can still look large.
taper_info_sessions: Session types are convention, not measurement. The papers prescribe maintained intensity and frequency, so the plan keeps your number of runs, one long run per week until race week, and one short race-pace sharpener per week — with every run scaled down with its week. The day-before shakeout with strides and the rest day two days out are running practice rather than a published protocol, and the evidence for priming with a short session the day before is small and variable.
taper_info_runners: For runners specifically, the largest data set available agrees with the shape and the length. Across 158,117 recreational marathoners (Smyth & Lawlor, Front Sports Act Living 2021;3:735220), tapers that cut volume every week out-performed tapers that did not, longer tapers beat shorter ones up to three weeks, and a strict three-week taper was worth a median 5 min 32 s (2.6%) against a minimal one. Those tapers were gentler than the meta-analysis optimum — roughly 30–40% off the normal week, with race week holding 35–50% of it — and this planner targets 33% (three weeks) or 38% (two weeks) in race week. Bosquet's pooled studies were mostly swimmers and cyclists (249 swimmers, 80 cyclists, 110 runners), so treat the volume numbers as a target and keep the intensity the papers insist on.
workout_warmup_blurb: Dynamic drills to switch your legs on before you run
workout_warmup_get_ready_text: Find a little space and stand tall. We start in fifteen seconds.
workout_warmup_march_text: March in place, easy and relaxed. Let your arms swing and find your breathing. This gently raises your temperature and wakes up your hips.
workout_warmup_shake_out_text: Loosen your shoulders and give your arms a good shake.
workout_warmup_arm_circles_text: Stretch your arms out to the sides. Circle them forward, starting small and growing bigger. I'll tell you when to reverse.
workout_warmup_reset_text: Feet hip-width apart. Roll your shoulders back and breathe.
workout_warmup_hip_circles_text: Hands on hips. Circle your hips round like you're stirring a big pot. Start small and keep it smooth.
workout_warmup_find_support_text: Move next to a wall, a post, anything you can hold on to.
workout_warmup_leg_swings_text: Stand on one leg and hold the support. Swing the free leg forward and back like a pendulum, controlled, letting the range grow a little. We switch legs halfway.
workout_warmup_stay_by_wall_text: Turn to face the wall, both hands on it.
workout_warmup_side_leg_swings_text: Keep your hands on the wall and a slight forward lean. Swing one leg across your body and out to the side, sweeping a bigger arc each time. We switch halfway.
workout_warmup_squats_text: Feet shoulder-width apart. Sit back and down like you're reaching for a chair, chest up, knees over your toes. Rise and repeat at an easy pace.
workout_warmup_almost_there_text: Stand tall. Strong and controlled on the next one.
workout_warmup_reverse_lunges_text: Step one leg back and lower until both knees are bent about ninety degrees, front knee over your ankle. Push back up to standing and alternate legs at a steady, controlled pace.
workout_warmup_two_to_go_text: Quick feet now. Light and bouncy.
workout_warmup_high_knees_text: Jog in place, driving your knees up to hip height. Land softly on the balls of your feet, quick but relaxed.
workout_warmup_butt_kicks_text: Jog in place again, this time kicking your heels up toward your glutes. Stay quick and light, and let the arms swing.
workout_stretch_blurb: Static holds to unwind after your run
workout_stretch_get_ready_text: Let your breathing settle. Easy does it, we take it slow.
workout_stretch_walk_it_off_text: Keep walking at an easy pace and let your heart rate drift down. Roll the shoulders and breathe deep — never come to a dead stop after a run.
workout_stretch_find_wall_text: Move somewhere with a wall, rail or post to lean on.
workout_stretch_calf_text: Step one foot back, keep that leg straight and the heel pressed down, front knee bent. Lean gently in until you feel the big calf muscle lengthen. About thirty seconds each side.
workout_stretch_deep_calf_text: Stay in the same stance, but bend the back knee while keeping the heel down. This reaches the deep calf, the workhorse that pushes you off every step. About twenty-five seconds each side.
workout_stretch_roll_shoulders_text: Stand tall and roll the shoulders back a few times.
workout_stretch_quad_text: Balance on one leg, using the wall if you need it. Grab the other ankle and draw the heel toward your glute, knees together, hips square. About thirty seconds each side.
workout_stretch_to_the_floor_text: Find a spot to get down on the ground, or stay standing if you prefer.
workout_stretch_hip_flexor_text: Half-kneel with one foot forward and the back knee down. Tuck the tailbone under and shift the hips gently forward until you feel the front of the hip open. About thirty seconds each side.
workout_stretch_stay_where_you_are_text: Get comfortable on your back for the next one.
workout_stretch_hamstring_text: Lie on your back and raise one leg, holding it behind the thigh with a soft knee. Draw it toward you until you feel the hamstring lengthen. Keep the other leg bent. About thirty seconds each side.
workout_stretch_stay_lying_down_text: Keep the back long against the ground.
workout_stretch_figure_four_text: Still on your back: cross one ankle over the opposite knee, then pull that thigh toward your chest until you feel the glute. Head and shoulders stay down. About thirty seconds each side.
workout_stretch_sit_up_tall_text: Come up to a seated position, back straight.
workout_stretch_butterfly_text: Sit tall with the soles of your feet together and knees dropped out. Hold your ankles and lean forward from the hips with a long, flat back. Breathe into it.
workouts_choose_hint: Two guided workouts with a spoken coach.
workouts_overview: About {minutes} minutes · {exercises} exercises · spoken coaching, so keep your sound on
yt_offline: You are offline. These videos stream from YouTube, so they need a connection.
yt_info_criteria: Not by view count alone. Every video is made for runners, is a follow-along session rather than a talk about one, and is led by a running coach, a physical therapist or a channel whose audience is known for its warm reception. Where an independent round-up (Coach magazine, Road Runner Sports) recommended a video, that counted too.
yt_info_privacy: Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play, and the player then runs in YouTube’s privacy-enhanced mode (youtube-nocookie.com).
yt_group_warm_up_blurb: Dynamic moves that raise your temperature and wake up hips, ankles and calves. Five to seven minutes.
yt_group_stretch_title: Stretch and yoga after the run
yt_group_stretch_blurb: Slow, held work for hips, hamstrings and calves once you are back home.
yt_group_strength_blurb: Two sessions a week on non-run or easy days. Bodyweight to start; add load as they get easy.
yt_why_QzmsKIdsgko: Run-specific coaching channel; goes from general movement to run-form drills, and you follow along in real time.
yt_why_MKuZOwYukho: A compact, moving (not held) sequence from one of the best-loved yoga channels on YouTube. Friendly to beginners.
yt_why_3WUtJxLv_wI: A no-equipment dynamic warm-up done in real time, aimed at getting you out the door ready and running pain-free.
yt_why_BylKeXx0fbc: Picked in Coach magazine’s round-up of post-run stretch videos. Short, and aimed squarely at hips and hamstrings.
yt_why_0hTllAb4XGg: A longer release-and-recover practice for after a run, with the calm, clear cueing the channel is known for.
yt_why_FbmLx_PahO4: Yoga-inspired cool-down for glutes, quads, hamstrings and hips, then spine and side body. Needs only a mat.
yt_why_pe9v9uiUujQ: Led by a running physical therapist (DPT, PhD). Seven staple exercises chosen for injury resistance.
yt_why_6LB__vPvaaE: Coached by Runna’s head coach Ben Parker: a leg-focused session built around what runners actually load.
yt_why_rZpMnnN4s_o: Bodyweight only, led by running coach Aaliyah Earvin; recommended by Road Runner Sports’ list of YouTube workouts for runners.
pain_map_hint: Tap the spot. Every dot marks a place running injuries show up — either side works.
pain_why_and_helps: Why it happens and what helps
pain_start_text: Pick a spot on the front, the back or the sole of the foot to see the running injuries that most often cause pain there: what each one feels like, why it happens and what helps.
pain_top_hint: Share of new running injuries, from a 2021 systematic review (Kakouris et al.).
pain_info_title: How to read this, and where it comes from
pain_info_guide: This is a guide, not a diagnosis. For the spot you pick it lists the running injuries that most often hurt there — the common ones first, then rarer ones worth ruling out — and what tells them apart. Only an examination can say which it is: see a sports physiotherapist or doctor when pain changes how you run or lasts more than a couple of weeks.
pain_info_overload: Most running pain is overload: training that outpaces what bone, tendon or muscle has adapted to. In a study that followed 5,200 runners, a single run more than 10% longer than the longest of the previous 30 days raised the injury rate (Frandsen et al. 2025); novices who raised their weekly distance by more than 30% got more overuse injuries such as runner’s knee, ITB syndrome and shin splints (Nielsen et al. 2014).
pain_info_running_with_pain: Running with pain: for tendon and kneecap pain, pain of up to about 5 out of 10 during a run that has settled by the next morning is a well-tested rule for carrying on (Silbernagel et al. 2007). It does not apply to a suspected stress fracture — that needs rest and a doctor — and many stress fractures come from eating too little for the training you do (IOC consensus on relative energy deficiency in sport, 2023).
pain_info_knees: Running doesn’t wear out your knees: across 17 studies and 114,829 people, recreational runners had less hip and knee arthritis (3.5%) than people who did not run (10.2%) (Alentorn-Geli et al. 2017).
pain_info_sources: Sources: injury shares from Kakouris et al. 2021 (systematic review); knee from the 2016 patellofemoral pain consensus; shins from Winters 2018 and Newman 2013; Achilles from the 2018 clinical practice guideline; heel from the 2023 guideline; hip from the LEAP trial (2018); high-risk stress fractures from McInnis & Ramey 2016; side stitch from Morton & Callister 2015; cardiac arrest in races from Kim et al. 2012.
pain_cause_pfp_stat: The most reported running injury: 16.7% of injuries in surveys
pain_cause_pfp_feels: A dull ache around or behind the kneecap, often in both knees. Stairs (especially going down), squatting, kneeling, hills and sitting for a long time with bent knees make it worse.
pain_cause_pfp_why: The joint behind the kneecap is taking more load than it is used to — usually after a jump in distance, hills or pace. Weak hip and thigh muscles are linked to it.
pain_cause_pfp_helps: Cut back to running that keeps the pain mild and settled by the next morning rather than stopping outright. Hip and thigh strengthening is the best-supported treatment; taping or foot orthoses can help in the short term. Raising your cadence by 5–10% lowers the load on the knee.
pain_cause_pfp_check: The knee swells, locks or gives way, or the pain started with a twist or a fall.
pain_cause_patellarTendinopathy_feels: Pain pinpointed on the tendon just below the kneecap. It hurts when the tendon works hard — hills, fast running, hopping — is often stiff at the start, eases as you warm up and is sorer afterwards or the next day.
pain_cause_patellarTendinopathy_why: Tendon overload, usually from adding speed work, hills or jumping faster than the tendon can adapt.
pain_cause_patellarTendinopathy_helps: Keep the tendon loaded, just less: trim the hills and speed, then rebuild with a progressive programme — holds such as wall sits, then slow heavy squats, then faster, springier work. Rest alone rarely fixes a tendon.
pain_cause_patellarTendinopathy_check: It isn’t improving after 6–8 weeks of sensible loading, or the knee swells.
pain_cause_itbs_feels: Sharp or burning pain on the outside of the knee that starts at a predictable point into a run and builds until you have to stop. Downhills and stairs make it worse; walking on the flat is usually fine.
pain_cause_itbs_why: Repeated compression of the band against the outside of the thigh bone at about 30° of knee bend. A quick rise in mileage, downhill running, always running the same way round a track or on a cambered road, and weak hip muscles are all linked to it.
pain_cause_itbs_helps: Back off the runs that bring it on — long runs and downhills first — and build hip strength. Return with short, flat runs. A slightly higher cadence reduces the strain. Foam rolling may ease it briefly but does not lengthen the band.
pain_cause_itbs_check: It hasn’t improved in 6 weeks, or the knee swells, clicks or locks — that points to the meniscus instead.
pain_cause_pesAnserine_feels: Tenderness on the inner side of the shin bone, a few centimetres below the knee joint. Worse on stairs, getting up from a chair and at night with the knees pressed together.
pain_cause_pesAnserine_why: Overload of the three tendons (and the bursa beneath them) that attach there. More common in women, older runners and knees with arthritis.
pain_cause_pesAnserine_helps: Ease off the runs and stairs that aggravate it for a while, sleep with a pillow between the knees, and strengthen the thigh and hip muscles.
pain_cause_pesAnserine_check: The knee joint itself swells, or the pain lasts beyond 6 weeks.
pain_cause_meniscus_feels: Pain right on the joint line at the side of the knee, often after a twist or a deep squat. Swelling that builds over hours, catching, clicking, or the knee locking and not fully straightening.
pain_cause_meniscus_why: A tear in the cartilage pad between thigh and shin bone — from a twist when younger, or gradual wear from about 40 onwards, often with no single event.
pain_cause_meniscus_helps: Worn (degenerative) tears do as well with exercise therapy as with keyhole surgery. Avoid twisting and deep squats for now, keep the knee moving and strengthen the thigh.
pain_cause_meniscus_check: The knee locks, won’t straighten fully, gives way or swells quickly.
pain_cause_mtss_feels: A diffuse ache along the inner edge of the shin bone, usually its lower two-thirds, tender along a strip at least 5 cm long. Often sore at the start of a run, easing as you warm up, then aching afterwards.
pain_cause_mtss_why: The shin bone is loaded faster than it can adapt — typically in new runners or after a jump in volume. Being female, a previous episode, a higher BMI and a flatter, more mobile arch all raise the risk.
pain_cause_mtss_helps: Cut running to a pain-free level and keep fit with cycling or pool running, then build back gradually. Calf and foot strength work helps the leg absorb load. Most cases settle within weeks of managing the load.
pain_cause_mtss_check: The pain narrows to one fingertip-sized spot, hopping on the leg hurts, or it aches at rest or at night — that points to a stress fracture.
pain_cause_tibialStressFracture_feels: A pinpoint, fingertip-sized tender spot on the shin bone that gets worse run by run, then hurts when walking and eventually at rest or at night. Hopping on that leg hurts.
pain_cause_tibialStressFracture_why: Bone breaking down faster than it rebuilds: a rapid increase in training, too little recovery and — above all — not eating enough for the training you do. Missed periods, low vitamin D and a previous stress fracture raise the risk.
pain_cause_tibialStressFracture_helps: Stop running and get it assessed; an MRI confirms it. Most heal with several weeks of relative rest (pain-free walking is usually fine) and a gradual return. Fuel your training properly.
pain_cause_tibialStressFracture_check: See a doctor before you run on it again.
pain_cause_anteriorTibialStressFracture_: Stress fracture at the front of the shin
A sore, tender spot on the sharp front edge of the shin bone, usually mid-shin, that worsens with running and jumping and may ache at night.
The front of the shin is the bone’s tension side: fractures there heal slowly and can progress to a complete break, which makes it a high-risk site.
Stop running and see a sports doctor promptly. It usually needs longer protection than other shin stress fractures, and sometimes surgery.
See a doctor before you run on it again.
pain_cause_cecs_feels: A tight, bursting or cramping pressure in the muscle (not the bone) that builds at the same time or distance into every run, sometimes with numbness or tingling in the foot or a slapping foot. It fades within minutes of stopping and often affects both legs.
pain_cause_cecs_why: The muscle swells with exercise inside a sheath of fascia that doesn’t stretch enough, so the pressure rises and squeezes the blood vessels and nerves.
pain_cause_cecs_helps: Changing technique to land further forward on the foot relieved symptoms in a small trial. Otherwise it needs a sports physician: the diagnosis is made by measuring the pressure in the muscle compartment, and persistent cases are treated with surgery.
pain_cause_cecs_check: It comes back on every run, or you notice numbness or foot weakness.
pain_cause_calfStrain_feels: Upper calf: a sudden sharp pain as if kicked, often during speed work or hills. Lower calf (soleus): a tightness that builds during a longer run until you have to stop. Tender to press; pushing off hurts.
pain_cause_calfStrain_why: A muscle tear under load. Age over 40, a previous calf strain and quick increases in volume or speed are the main risk factors.
pain_cause_calfStrain_helps: Keep walking if it is comfortable and start calf loading early — seated, bent-knee heel raises for the lower calf, straight-knee ones for the upper — then return with graded runs.
pain_cause_calfStrain_check: The calf swells or feels warm, or the pain doesn’t ease — rule out a blood clot.
pain_cause_cramp_feels: A sudden, involuntary, rock-hard spasm — usually the calf or hamstring — late in a hard race or long run. It stops within minutes but can leave the muscle sore.
pain_cause_cramp_why: Mostly neuromuscular fatigue: the reflexes controlling a tired muscle misfire. Dehydration and salt loss are weakly linked at best. Having cramped before is the strongest predictor.
pain_cause_cramp_helps: Stop and gently stretch the cramping muscle. Prevent it by pacing realistically and training at your race intensity and duration.
pain_cause_cramp_check: Cramps come at rest or very often, or with confusion, vomiting or dark urine.
pain_cause_dvt_feels: One calf (and often the ankle) swells and feels warm, tight or tender, and may look red — a cramp-like ache that doesn’t ease with stretching or rest. Often after a long flight or drive, surgery or a leg injury.
pain_cause_dvt_why: A clot in a deep leg vein. Fit athletes get them too and they are easily mistaken for a calf strain. Long travel to and from races, dehydration, hormonal contraception and recent injury raise the risk.
pain_cause_dvt_helps: This is a medical problem, not a training one: it needs a scan and blood-thinning treatment.
pain_cause_dvt_check: See a doctor the same day. Call emergency services if you also have chest pain or sudden breathlessness — the clot may have reached the lungs.
pain_cause_doms_feels: Stiff, tender muscles in both legs that start 12–24 hours after a hard, long or unusual session — a race, a hilly run — and peak at 24–72 hours. Going downstairs is the giveaway. Gone within a week.
pain_cause_doms_why: Unaccustomed eccentric work — muscles braking while they lengthen, above all running downhill — causes micro-damage. One bout protects you from the next for weeks (the repeated-bout effect).
pain_cause_doms_helps: Time. Easy movement feels better and massage helps a little; nothing reliably speeds recovery. It isn’t an injury, but don’t race hard again until it has gone.
pain_cause_doms_check: The pain is in one spot of one leg, the muscle swells a lot, or your urine turns dark brown — that last one needs a doctor straight away.
pain_cause_hipFlexor_feels: Pain deep in the front of the hip or groin when lifting the knee — climbing stairs, getting into a car, running uphill or fast. Stretching the front of the hip may pull on it.
pain_cause_hipFlexor_why: Overload of the hip flexors, often after adding hills, speed work or strides.
pain_cause_hipFlexor_helps: Ease off hills and speed, then strengthen the hip flexors progressively, for example standing knee lifts against a band. Most settle within a few weeks.
pain_cause_hipFlexor_check: The pain is deep, worsens with each run or hurts when you hop — rule out a stress fracture first.
pain_cause_hipJoint_feels: Deep groin pain, often felt as a grip around the side of the hip, with catching, clicking or locking. Low seats, putting on socks and deep bending hurt.
pain_cause_hipJoint_why: The shape of the hip bones can pinch the joint rim (the labrum) in deep bending; running adds repetitive load.
pain_cause_hipJoint_helps: Avoid deep hip bending for now. Hip and trunk strengthening, guided by a physiotherapist, is the first-line treatment.
pain_cause_hipJoint_check: Catching or locking persists, or the pain limits your walking.
pain_cause_adductor_feels: Pain in the inner groin near the pubic bone, tender on the inner-thigh tendon, worse squeezing the knees together, changing direction or sprinting.
pain_cause_adductor_why: Overload of the inner-thigh muscles — commoner in kicking and cutting sports, but also seen after speed work and trail running.
pain_cause_adductor_helps: Progressive adductor strengthening, such as the Copenhagen side plank, both treats and prevents it.
pain_cause_adductor_check: A lump in the groin appears when you cough, or the pain lasts beyond 6 weeks.
pain_cause_femoralNeckStressFracture_fee: A vague, deep ache in the groin or front of the hip that gets worse with running, then with walking. You may limp, and hopping on the leg hurts — but pressing on it usually doesn’t, as the bone is deep.
pain_cause_femoralNeckStressFracture_why: Bone overload, most often in distance runners who are under-fuelled, have missed periods or have had a stress fracture before.
pain_cause_femoralNeckStressFracture_hel: Stop running and see a doctor within days — an X-ray can miss it, so MRI is used. Caught early it heals with rest; missed, it can break completely.
pain_cause_femoralNeckStressFracture_che: See a doctor promptly — immediately if you can’t bear weight.
pain_cause_glutealTendinopathy_feels: Pain on the bony point on the outside of the hip, tender to press. Lying on that side, standing on one leg, stairs, crossing your legs and getting up after sitting all aggravate it.
pain_cause_glutealTendinopathy_why: The gluteal tendons are squeezed and overloaded where they wrap around the hip bone — most common in women over 40 and after mileage increases.
pain_cause_glutealTendinopathy_helps: Education plus progressive glute strengthening beat a steroid injection in the LEAP trial (77% vs 58% better at 8 weeks). Avoid squeezing the tendons: don’t cross your legs or hang on one hip, and sleep with a pillow between your knees.
pain_cause_glutealTendinopathy_check: The pain spreads into the groin or you start to limp.
pain_cause_quadStrain_feels: A sudden sharp or pulling pain in the front of the thigh during a sprint, strides or a kick, then tenderness at one spot and sometimes bruising.
pain_cause_quadStrain_why: A muscle tear, usually during fast running when the muscle is tired or not warmed up.
pain_cause_quadStrain_helps: A few days of relative rest, then progressive strengthening and a graded return to faster running.
pain_cause_quadStrain_check: You felt a pop, there is a dent in the muscle, or you can’t lift the leg.
pain_cause_hamstringStrain_feels: A sudden sharp or pulling pain in the back of the thigh during a sprint, strides or a fast finish, sometimes with a pop. Tender at one spot, bruising after a day or two.
pain_cause_hamstringStrain_why: The muscle tears while braking the swinging leg at speed. Fatigue, a previous strain and little fast running in training raise the risk.
pain_cause_hamstringStrain_helps: Start gentle loading within days and progress to heavier and faster work. The Nordic hamstring exercise halves the rate of hamstring injuries.
pain_cause_hamstringStrain_check: You felt a pop high up near the sit bone, there is a large bruise, or you can’t walk normally — the tendon may have torn off the bone.
pain_cause_proximalHamstring_feels: A deep ache at the sit bone, low in the buttock. Sitting on hard chairs, driving, uphill running, speed work and long strides make it worse; it may ease once warm but is sorer afterwards.
pain_cause_proximalHamstring_why: The hamstring tendon is overloaded and compressed against the sit bone — typically after adding hills or speed.
pain_cause_proximalHamstring_helps: Cut hills and speed, sit on a cushion and skip hamstring stretches, which compress the tendon. Start with holds and progress to heavier hamstring strengthening.
pain_cause_proximalHamstring_check: It started with a sudden pop, or the leg feels numb or weak.
pain_cause_deepGluteal_feels: Deep buttock pain, worse after sitting a while, that may spread down the back of the thigh like sciatica, with tingling.
pain_cause_deepGluteal_why: The sciatic nerve is irritated where it passes the deep hip muscles in the buttock. The lower back causes the same pattern far more often, so it is ruled out first.
pain_cause_deepGluteal_helps: Break up long sitting, keep moving, and see a physiotherapist for nerve and hip-muscle work.
pain_cause_deepGluteal_check: Numbness or weakness is getting worse.
pain_cause_lowBackPain_feels: An ache or stiffness across the lower back, sometimes one-sided, that changes with position and activity, without pain shooting below the knee.
pain_cause_lowBackPain_why: Usually no single structural cause. Running doesn’t make it more likely: back pain is less common in runners, and runners’ spinal discs are better hydrated than non-runners’.
pain_cause_lowBackPain_helps: Keep moving — easy running and walking are usually fine and likely help. Add trunk and hip strength work; avoid long bed rest.
pain_cause_lowBackPain_check: The pain is constant and worse at night, comes with fever or weight loss, or followed a fall — or, in a teenager, gets worse leaning backwards (a spine stress fracture).
pain_cause_sciatica_name: Pain referred from the lower back
pain_cause_sciatica_feels: Pain that travels from the lower back or buttock down the back of the thigh, sometimes past the knee, with tingling, numbness or weakness. Bending, sitting or coughing can set it off.
pain_cause_sciatica_why: An irritated nerve root in the lower spine: the leg hurts, but the source is the back.
pain_cause_sciatica_helps: Most cases settle within weeks. Stay active — walk, and run if it is tolerable — and see a physiotherapist.
pain_cause_sciatica_check: Numbness around the groin or buttocks, new bladder or bowel trouble, or weakness in both legs is an emergency — get help straight away.
pain_cause_stitch_stat: About 70% of runners get one in a year
pain_cause_stitch_feels: A sharp, well-localised pain just under the ribs on one side, sometimes with pain at the tip of the shoulder. Worse at speed and downhill; gone within minutes of stopping.
pain_cause_stitch_why: Most likely irritation of the lining of the abdominal wall. Eating or drinking a lot — especially sugary drinks — in the 2–3 hours before a run raises the risk, and it is commoner in younger runners.
pain_cause_stitch_helps: Avoid big meals and large sugary drinks before running. When it strikes, slow down, breathe deeply, push firmly on the spot and bend forward, or tighten your stomach muscles.
pain_cause_stitch_check: The pain continues after you stop, keeps getting worse, or comes with fever, vomiting or blood — that isn’t a stitch.
pain_cause_nippleChafing_feels: Stinging, raw and sometimes bleeding nipples after a long run. Commoner with high mileage and cotton shirts.
pain_cause_nippleChafing_why: Hours of the shirt rubbing over sweaty skin.
pain_cause_nippleChafing_helps: Cover them with plasters or tape, or use a lubricant, and wear a technical (non-cotton) shirt or a well-fitting sports bra.
pain_cause_nippleChafing_check: There are signs of infection, or a discharge or lump that has nothing to do with running.
pain_cause_cardiac_aka: a warning sign, not an injury
pain_cause_cardiac_feels: Pressure, tightness, squeezing or pain in the chest while running, possibly spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back, with breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations or fainting.
pain_cause_cardiac_why: It can mean the heart muscle isn’t getting enough blood, or an inherited heart condition. Cardiac arrest in races is rare — about 1 in 185,000 half- and full-marathon runners — but chest symptoms must never be run through.
pain_cause_cardiac_helps: Stop running. Don’t try to finish the run or the race.
pain_cause_cardiac_check: Call emergency services now. If it has already passed, still see a doctor before you run again.
pain_cause_achilles_stat: The most common new running injury: 10.3%
pain_cause_achilles_feels: Pain and stiffness in the tendon 2–6 cm above the heel. Stiff first steps in the morning and at the start of a run, easing as you warm up, worse later or the next day. The tendon may feel thickened and tender to pinch.
pain_cause_achilles_why: Tendon overload — more mileage, hills or speed than the tendon has adapted to, especially with weaker calves. It gets more common with age.
pain_cause_achilles_helps: Progressive calf and tendon loading (heel raises, getting heavier) for at least 12 weeks has the strongest evidence. You can usually keep running if the pain stays at or below 5 out of 10 and has settled by the next morning.
pain_cause_achilles_check: You felt a sudden snap, as if kicked in the heel, and can’t rise onto your toes — a possible rupture: see a doctor the same day.
pain_cause_insertionalAchilles_feels: Pain at the back of the heel where the Achilles attaches, often with a bony bump that rubs on the shoe’s heel counter. Uphill running and calf stretches make it worse.
pain_cause_insertionalAchilles_why: The tendon is squeezed against the heel bone whenever the ankle bends up, on top of the usual tendon overload.
pain_cause_insertionalAchilles_helps: Heel lifts and shoes with a soft, low heel counter. Skip calf stretches off a step and don’t drop the heel below floor level; strengthen with heel raises on flat ground.
pain_cause_insertionalAchilles_check: Sudden pain with a snap, or you can’t rise onto your toes.
pain_cause_ankleSprain_feels: Sudden pain on the outside of the ankle after rolling the foot inwards — on a trail, kerb or pothole — followed by swelling and often bruising.
pain_cause_ankleSprain_why: The outer ankle ligaments are overstretched or torn. A previous sprain is the biggest risk factor for the next one.
pain_cause_ankleSprain_helps: Protect it for a few days but start moving and walking early, with a brace for the return to running. Balance and strength training roughly halves the chance of spraining it again.
pain_cause_ankleSprain_check: You can’t take four steps, or the bone is tender at the back edge or tip of either ankle bone or at the base of the little-toe bone (the Ottawa ankle rules) — get an X-ray.
pain_cause_peroneal_feels: An ache, sometimes with swelling, behind and below the outer ankle bone along the tendons to the outside of the foot. Worse on cambered roads and uneven trails.
pain_cause_peroneal_why: Overload of the tendons that steady the outside of the ankle — common after sprains, in unstable ankles and in high-arched feet.
pain_cause_peroneal_helps: Cut back on camber and trails for a while and strengthen the ankle — turning the foot outwards against a band — plus balance work.
pain_cause_peroneal_check: The tendon snaps or clicks over the ankle bone, or the swelling persists.
pain_cause_tibialisPosterior_feels: Pain, sometimes with swelling, behind and below the inner ankle bone, running on into the arch. A single-leg heel raise is weak or painful, and over time the arch may flatten.
pain_cause_tibialisPosterior_why: Overload of the tendon that holds up the arch — linked to rapid training increases and flat, mobile feet.
pain_cause_tibialisPosterior_helps: Reduce the running load, use arch support or orthoses for a while, and strengthen the tendon progressively with heel raises and resisted turning-in of the foot.
pain_cause_tibialisPosterior_check: The arch is visibly collapsing or you can no longer rise onto the toes of that foot.
pain_cause_plantarHeel_feels: Sharp pain under the inner front of the heel with the first steps in the morning or after sitting. It eases once you get going, then returns after long standing or at the end of the day.
pain_cause_plantarHeel_why: Overload of the thick band along the sole (the plantar fascia) where it attaches to the heel. Linked to sudden mileage increases, tight calves, a higher BMI and long hours on your feet.
pain_cause_plantarHeel_helps: Calf and plantar-fascia stretches, foot and ankle strengthening, taping and supportive shoes or inserts all have guideline support. It is slow, but most people recover within a year.
pain_cause_plantarHeel_check: The whole heel hurts and squeezing it from both sides is painful (a possible stress fracture), or there is numbness or tingling.
pain_cause_heelStressFracture_feels: Heel pain that gets worse as you run rather than easing, and pain when the heel is squeezed from both sides.
pain_cause_heelStressFracture_why: Repetitive impact on the heel bone, often after a quick mileage increase or when under-fuelled.
pain_cause_heelStressFracture_helps: Stop running and get it assessed. It usually heals with a period of protected walking and a gradual return.
pain_cause_heelStressFracture_check: See a doctor before you run on it again.
pain_cause_fatPad_feels: A deep, bruise-like ache in the centre of the heel, worse barefoot on hard floors and when landing on the heel — without the first-step pattern of plantar heel pain.
pain_cause_fatPad_why: The cushioning fat pad under the heel is bruised or has thinned, which it does with age.
pain_cause_fatPad_helps: Cushioned shoes, a heel cup, taping that gathers the pad under the heel, and softer surfaces for a while.
pain_cause_fatPad_check: It lasts beyond 6 weeks despite the extra cushioning.
pain_cause_navicularStressFracture_feels: A vague ache across the top and inner side of the midfoot that worsens with running and is hard to pin down. The bone on top of the midfoot is tender to press.
pain_cause_navicularStressFracture_why: A high-risk stress fracture: the navicular has a poor blood supply, so it heals slowly and often only shows up on CT or MRI.
pain_cause_navicularStressFracture_helps: Stop running and see a sports doctor. The usual treatment is about 6 weeks in a non-weight-bearing cast or boot.
pain_cause_navicularStressFracture_check: See a doctor before you run on it again.
pain_cause_metatarsalStressFracture_feel: Pain on the top of the forefoot, usually over the 2nd or 3rd toe bone, with swelling and a tender spot on the bone. It builds with each run and can hurt when walking.
pain_cause_metatarsalStressFracture_why: Repetitive loading of a long, thin bone, often after a jump in mileage, new shoes, a new surface or under-fuelling.
pain_cause_metatarsalStressFracture_help: Stop running and get it assessed. Most heal in 4–8 weeks in a stiff shoe or boot. The outer (5th) metatarsal is a high-risk site.
pain_cause_metatarsalStressFracture_chec: See a doctor before you run on it again.
pain_cause_extensorTendinopathy_feels: An ache along the tendons on the top of the foot, right under the laces, sometimes with a little swelling. Lifting the toes against resistance hurts.
pain_cause_extensorTendinopathy_why: Compression from tight laces or a stiff tongue — often after new shoes — or tight calves making the tendons work harder.
pain_cause_extensorTendinopathy_helps: Loosen the laces or skip the eyelets over the sore spot, pad the tongue, and ease back for a few days.
pain_cause_extensorTendinopathy_check: There is marked swelling or a tender spot on a bone — that could be a stress fracture instead.
pain_cause_metatarsalgia_feels: An aching, bruised feeling under the ball of the foot, behind the 2nd to 4th toes, worse barefoot on hard floors and when running fast or on your toes.
pain_cause_metatarsalgia_why: Too much pressure through the ends of the long foot bones — linked to high or stiff arches, thin cushioning and tight calves.
pain_cause_metatarsalgia_helps: A metatarsal pad placed just behind the sore area, more cushioned shoes, calf stretches and toe-strength work.
pain_cause_metatarsalgia_check: One bone is tender to press on top, or the foot swells — rule out a stress fracture.
pain_cause_morton_feels: Burning, electric or numb feelings between two toes — usually the 3rd and 4th — and the sense of a pebble in the shoe. Tight, narrow shoes bring it on; taking the shoe off and rubbing the foot relieves it.
pain_cause_morton_why: A thickened, irritated nerve squeezed between the ends of two foot bones.
pain_cause_morton_helps: Shoes with a wider toe box, looser forefoot lacing and a metatarsal pad behind the sore spot. Injections or surgery only if that fails.
pain_cause_morton_check: The numbness stays after running or keeps spreading.
pain_cause_sesamoiditis_feels: Pain under the big toe joint on the ball of the foot when pushing off, running on your toes or bending the big toe upwards.
pain_cause_sesamoiditis_why: Two small bones inside the tendon under the big toe take much of the load at push-off; hills, speed work and thin shoes overload them.
pain_cause_sesamoiditis_helps: Offload the spot with a pad cut out around it, wear stiffer-soled shoes, and cut speed and hill work for a while.
pain_cause_sesamoiditis_check: It hasn’t eased in 2–3 weeks or is sharply painful to press — a sesamoid stress fracture needs imaging.
pain_cause_bigToeArthritis_feels: Pain and stiffness in the big toe joint itself, often a bony bump on top, and a toe that won’t bend up far — noticed at push-off and uphill.
pain_cause_bigToeArthritis_why: Wear of the joint cartilage, usually from middle age.
pain_cause_bigToeArthritis_helps: Stiffer or rocker-soled shoes reduce how far the joint bends; a physio or podiatrist can add mobility work and inserts.
pain_cause_bigToeArthritis_check: The joint turns suddenly red, hot and swollen — that can be gout.
pain_cause_blackToenail_feels: A toenail — usually the big or second toe — turns purple-black after a long or downhill run. It throbs while fresh and is painless later; it may fall off and regrow over months.
pain_cause_blackToenail_why: The toe repeatedly hits the front of the shoe and bleeds under the nail.
pain_cause_blackToenail_helps: Shoes with a thumb’s width of room at the front, heel-lock lacing to stop the foot sliding forward, and short-trimmed nails. A painless black nail can be left alone.
pain_cause_blackToenail_check: The throbbing is severe (the blood can be released), it looks infected, or a dark streak appears without any injury — have that checked for skin cancer.
pain_cause_blisters_feels: A stinging hot spot that becomes a fluid-filled bubble, typically on the toes, heel or ball of the foot.
pain_cause_blisters_why: Friction and shear between skin, sock and shoe, made worse by moisture — one of the commonest skin injuries at marathons.
pain_cause_blisters_helps: Moisture-wicking synthetic socks, well-fitting shoes, and lubricant or tape on known hot spots. Leave small blisters intact; drain big ones with a sterile needle and keep the roof on.
pain_cause_blisters_check: Redness spreads, or pus or red streaks appear — especially if you have diabetes.
pain_spot_side_stitch_where: Just below the ribs, on one side of the abdomen.
pain_spot_lower_back_where: Across the lower back, above the buttocks.
pain_spot_groin_name: Groin and front of the hip
pain_spot_groin_where: The crease where the thigh meets the body, and the inner groin.
pain_spot_outer_hip_where: The bony point on the side of the hip.
pain_spot_buttock_where: Deep in the middle of the buttock.
pain_spot_sit_bone_where: Low in the buttock, the bone you sit on.
pain_spot_front_thigh_where: The quadriceps, between hip and knee.
pain_spot_back_thigh_where: The hamstrings, between buttock and knee.
pain_spot_front_knee_where: Around, behind or just below the kneecap.
pain_spot_outer_knee_where: The outer side of the knee joint.
pain_spot_inner_knee_where: The inner side of the knee joint and just below it.
pain_spot_inner_shin_where: Along the inner border of the shin bone, lower two-thirds.
pain_spot_outer_shin_name: Front and outside of the shin
pain_spot_outer_shin_where: The muscle beside the sharp front edge of the shin, and the edge itself.
pain_spot_calf_where: The muscle at the back of the lower leg.
pain_spot_achilles_where: The cord at the back of the ankle, 2–6 cm above the heel.
pain_spot_back_heel_where: Where the Achilles tendon attaches to the heel bone.
pain_spot_outer_ankle_where: Around and below the outer ankle bone.
pain_spot_inner_ankle_where: Around and below the inner ankle bone.
pain_spot_top_of_foot_where: The top of the midfoot and forefoot, under the laces.
pain_spot_big_toe_joint_where: The ball of the foot behind the big toe.
pain_spot_ball_of_foot_where: Under the forefoot, behind the 2nd to 5th toes.
pain_spot_arch_where: The inner, raised middle of the sole.
pain_view_front_caption: Front of the body, facing you
pain_view_front_map: Body map, front of the body, facing you
pain_view_back_map: Body map, back of the body
pain_view_sole_map: Body map, sole of either foot
pain_red_flag_chest: Chest pain or pressure, fainting or sudden breathlessness while running: stop and call emergency services.
pain_red_flag_weight: You can’t put weight on the leg or walk normally.
pain_red_flag_bone: A fingertip-sized spot on a bone hurts to press, or hopping on the leg hurts.
pain_red_flag_rest: Pain at rest or at night, or pain that gets worse run after run.
pain_red_flag_swelling: Swelling, warmth or redness — above all of one calf — or a fever.
pain_red_flag_pop: A pop or snap followed by pain and loss of function.
pain_tool_metronome: Raise your cadence with the metronome
